questions.stem: What is \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{4x+1}\,dx\)?
questions.hint: Rewrite the square root as a fractional power \((4x+1)^{1/2}\), and remember the reverse chain rule needs an extra division by the derivative of \(4x+1\) (which is 4).

steps.explain: Rewrite the square root as a fractional power, then apply the reverse chain rule to find the primitive of \((4x+1)^{1/2}\).
Evaluate at the upper limit \(x=2\) and the lower limit \(x=0\).
Evaluate \(9^{3/2} = (\sqrt9)^3 = 27\), then combine the fractions.

Option B comes from forgetting the extra factor of 4 in the reverse chain rule denominator (using \(\div\tfrac32\) only, not \(\div\tfrac32\times4\)), giving \(\dfrac23(27-1)=\dfrac{52}{3}\). Option C comes from forgetting to subtract the lower-limit value entirely (\(\tfrac{27}{6}=\tfrac92\)). Option D comes from doubling the denominator by mistake (\(\tfrac{26}{12}=\tfrac{13}{6}\)).

questions.stem: Evaluate \( \displaystyle\int_0^2 (3x^4+2x)\,dx \).

steps.explain: Find the primitive of each term using \( \int x^n\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \).
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus: evaluate the primitive at the upper limit \( x=2 \) and subtract its value at the lower limit \( x=0 \).
Simplify the fraction and combine with the whole number.

Check (D): \( \cos x \) is even and \( 4x^4 \) is also even, so neither integrates to zero over a symmetric interval — only the odd term \( -x^3 \) does. Pitfall: assuming any symmetric-interval integral is automatically 0 ignores that only odd functions have this property.

questions.stem: Find the primitive function of \(\displaystyle\int \left(2x^3+\dfrac{1}{3x+1}\right)dx\).
questions.hint: Integrate each term separately: \(\int 2x^3\,dx\) is a power rule; \(\int \dfrac{1}{3x+1}\,dx\) needs the reverse chain rule with \(\ln\).

steps.explain: Integrate the first term using the power rule.
Integrate the second term: for \(\int \dfrac{1}{ax+b}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{a}\ln|ax+b|+C\), here \(a=3\).
Combine both results with a single constant of integration.

questions.stem: Find the primitive function of \(\displaystyle\int \left(\sin 10x - \dfrac{2}{e^{5x}}\right)dx\).
questions.hint: Rewrite \(\dfrac{2}{e^{5x}}\) as \(2e^{-5x}\) first, then integrate each term with the reverse chain rule.

steps.explain: Rewrite the second term with a negative exponent so the reverse chain rule is easier to apply.
Integrate \(\sin 10x\): \(\int \sin(ax)\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{a}\cos(ax)\).
Integrate \(-2e^{-5x}\): \(\int e^{ax}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{a}e^{ax}\), here \(a=-5\).
Combine both results.

Substitute the given point \( P(2,4) \) — meaning \( x=2, y=4 \) — to find \( C \).
Solve the resulting equation for \( C \).
Substitute \( C=10 \) back into the general primitive to state the equation of the curve.

parts.stem: (b) Find the equation of the normal to the curve at \( P \), in the form \( ax+by+c=0 \), where \( a, b, c \) are integers.

steps.explain: Find the gradient of the tangent at \( P(2,4) \) by substituting \( x=2 \) into \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^3+2x-7 \).
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal.
Use the point–gradient formula \( y-y_1=m(x-x_1) \) with \( P(2,4) \) and \( m=-\tfrac15 \).
Multiply both sides by 5 to clear the fraction, then rearrange into \( ax+by+c=0 \) form with integer coefficients.
Part (a): integrate \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) term by term to find \(y\) in terms of \(x\), including a constant of integration.
Use the given point P(2, 4) on the curve to solve for \(C\).
Part (b): find the gradient of the tangent at P by substituting \(x=2\) into the original derivative \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x^3+2x-7\).
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.
Use the point-gradient form with P(2, 4) and normal gradient \(-\dfrac{1}{5}\), then rearrange into \(ax+by+c=0\) form.

questions.stem: Consider the graph of \(y=\ln(x+r)\) shown below, where \(r>1\). The shaded region bound by the curve, the coordinate axes and the line \(x=t\) (where \(t>0\)) is used to model a garden.

steps.explain: Start with the given equation and rearrange to make \(x\) the subject, first undoing the logarithm by raising \(e\) to the power of each side.
Subtract \(r\) from both sides.

parts.stem: (b) Show that the area of this region, \(A\), in terms of \(r\) and \(t\) is \(A = (t+r)\ln(t+r) - r\ln r - t\).

steps.explain: Since \(\ln(x+r)\) cannot be integrated directly (as a function of \(x\)) at this level, integrate with respect to \(y\) instead, using the inverse relationship from part (a). The shaded area equals the rectangle of width \(t\) and height \(\ln(t+r)\), minus the area under \(x=e^y-r\) between \(y=\ln r\) and \(y=\ln(t+r)\).
Find the primitive of \(e^y-r\) with respect to \(y\), and evaluate between the limits.
Evaluate the bracket at the upper limit \(y=\ln(t+r)\): since \(e^{\ln(t+r)}=t+r\).
Evaluate the bracket at the lower limit \(y=\ln r\): since \(e^{\ln r}=r\).
Subtract the lower-limit value from the upper-limit value, then substitute back into the area expression and simplify.
steps.work: \(A = t\ln(t+r) - \Big[(t+r-r\ln(t+r)) - (r-r\ln r)\Big] = t\ln(t+r) - t - r + r\ln(t+r) + r - r\ln r\)

steps.explain: Cancel the \(-r\) and \(+r\), then combine the two \(\ln(t+r)\) terms.

questions.stem: The function \(f(x)=x(x-2)(x-6)\) is given. The diagram shows the area bounded by the graph of \(y=f(x)\) and the x-axis.

parts.hint: Find the three roots where the curve intersects the x-axis, expand f(x), and integrate each section separately taking the absolute value of the region below the axis.

steps.explain:
Find the \(x\)-intercepts by setting \(f(x) = 0\), and expand \(f(x)\) for integration.
The curve intersects the \(x\)-axis at three points: \(x = 0\), \(x = 2\), and \(x = 6\). Expanding gives \(f(x) = x^3 - 8x^2 + 12x\).

Determine where \(f(x)\) is above and below the \(x\)-axis to set up the area integrals.
- On \([0, 2]\), \(f(x) \ge 0\) (above the axis), so \(A_1 = \int_0^2 f(x)\,dx\).
- On \([2, 6]\), \(f(x) \le 0\) (below the axis), so its signed integral is negative: \(A_2 = -\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = \left|\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx\right|\).

Find the antiderivative \(F(x)\) and evaluate the area \(A_1\) over \([0, 2]\).
Integrate term by term to obtain \(F(x) = \frac{x^4}{4} - \frac{8x^3}{3} + 6x^2\).

Evaluate the integral over \([2, 6]\), negate it to obtain the positive geometric area \(A_2\), and add both areas.
Evaluating \(F(6)\) yields \(-36\), giving \(\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = -36 - \frac{20}{3} = -\frac{128}{3}\).

parts.stem: Let \(g(x)=f(ax+b)\). Find \(a\) and \(b\) if \(\int_4^0g(x)\,dx+\int_4^6g(x)\,dx\) has the same area calculated in the previous part.
parts.hint: Reverse the reversed integration limits in the first integral: ∫₄⁰ g(x) dx = −∫₀⁴ g(x) dx. Observe which lobes of f(x) correspond to [0, 4] and [4, 6].

steps.explain:
Rewrite the given signed integrals with standard lower-to-upper limits.
Recall that reversing limits negates the integral: \(\int_4^0 g(x)\,dx = -\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx\).
Therefore, the expression becomes:
$$\int_4^0 g(x)\,dx + \int_4^6 g(x)\,dx = -\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx + \int_4^6 g(x)\,dx$$
For this sum to equal the positive area \(\frac{148}{3} = \frac{128}{3} + \frac{20}{3}\):
1. \(-\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx\) must equal \(+\frac{128}{3}\), meaning \(g(x) \le 0\) on \([0, 4]\).
2. \(\int_4^6 g(x)\,dx\) must equal \(+\frac{20}{3}\), meaning \(g(x) \ge 0\) on \([4, 6]\).
steps.work:
\(\int_4^0 g(x)\,dx + \int_4^6 g(x)\,dx = -\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx + \int_4^6 g(x)\,dx\\
-\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx = \frac{128}{3} \quad\text{and}\quad \int_4^6 g(x)\,dx = \frac{20}{3}\\
\text{Sum } = \frac{128}{3} + \frac{20}{3} = \frac{148}{3}\)

steps.explain:
Compare the lobe widths of \(f(u)\) and \(g(x)\) to determine the reflection factor \(a\).
- In \(f(u)\), the smaller lobe (area \(\frac{20}{3}\)) is on \([0, 2]\) (width 2), followed by the larger lobe (area \(\frac{128}{3}\)) on \([2, 6]\) (width 4).
- In \(g(x)\), the larger lobe (area \(\frac{128}{3}\)) is on \([0, 4]\) (width 4), followed by the smaller lobe (area \(\frac{20}{3}\)) on \([4, 6]\) (width 2).
Because the lobe widths and order are horizontally reversed without scale stretching, \(g(x)\) is a horizontal reflection of \(f\), so \(a = -1\).
steps.work:
\(\text{Original } f(u): [0, 2] \text{ (width 2)} \to [2, 6] \text{ (width 4)}\\
\text{Transformed } g(x): [0, 4] \text{ (width 4)} \to [4, 6] \text{ (width 2)}\\
\implies \text{Horizontal reflection with no scaling: } a = -1\)

steps.explain:
Solve for the horizontal translation \(b\) and verify the transformation.
With \(a = -1\), the argument is \(u = -x + b\).
- At \(x = 0\), \(u\) must equal the original rightmost root \(u = 6\): \(-0 + b = 6 \implies b = 6\).
- Check \(x = 4\): \(u = -4 + 6 = 2\) (matches intermediate root \(u = 2\)).
- Check \(x = 6\): \(u = -6 + 6 = 0\) (matches initial root \(u = 0\)).
Thus, \(g(x) = f(6 - x) = f(-x + 6)\), so \((a, b) = (-1, 6)\).
steps.work:
\(u = ax + b = -x + b\\
\text{At } x = 0:\; u = 6 \implies b = 6\\
\text{Check: } x = 4 \implies u = 2;\quad x = 6 \implies u = 0\\
\therefore \boxed{(a, b) = (-1, 6)}\)

questions.stem:
Isabelle is exploring the even function \( y = e^{-x^2} \), which has two points of inflection at B, C.

Using the Trapezoidal Rule with three function values, the approximation is:
\[ \int_B^C e^{-x^2}\,dx \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2e}} \]

Explain why Isabelle correctly knows that the true area satisfies:
\[ \int_B^C e^{-x^2}\,dx > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2e}} \]
options: The curve is concave down between the points of inflection, so the straight lines of the trapezoids lie entirely below the curve, making the approximation an underestimate.
The curve is concave up between the points of inflection, making the trapezoidal approximation an overestimate.
The Trapezoidal rule always provides an underestimate for symmetrical functions with a maximum at the origin.
The exact integral of any exponential function is always greater than any numerical approximation.

steps.explain: Consider the concavity of the curve between the points of inflection \( B \) and \( C \). We found \( y'' < 0 \) in this interval.
When a curve is concave down, any chord (straight line) connecting two points on the curve will lie below the curve.
